prose:e-132caf: What the health system needs to be able to do: the system needs to detect health events early — through case reporting, syndromic and event-based surveillance, and adverse-event and safety reporting — and to link those signals to verified people, providers, and places so that cases can be confirmed, de-duplicated, and located. It needs to turn signals into assessed risk and timely warning, increasingly by drawing weather, climate, and environmental data alongside health data so that climate-sensitive threats can be anticipated rather than only observed. And it needs to coordinate the response and share information across providers and, where required, across borders.
prose:e-a2a9c4: How to read the mapping: the spreadsheet that follows traces each capability from the goal through stakeholder value, business capability, and application service to the DPI-H components and foundational-DPI dependencies that support it, and notes where each component is reused by other goals. The goal rests heavily on shared infrastructure other goals already require — the client registry to link and de-duplicate cases, the health workforce registry to authenticate reporters, the health facility registry to geolocate events and map outbreaks, the terminology service for standardised disease and event coding, the product registry as the authoritative product reference for adverse-event and safety reporting, and the health management information system for aggregation and secondary use. Its distinctive DPI-H component is the public health surveillance platform; and, distinctively among the seven goals, its climate dimension draws on a foundational-DPI weather, climate, and environment data capability that sits outside the health sector and is reached through the same interoperability that connects the rest of the architecture. The operational systems that do the work — case-reporting, adverse-event, outbreak-management, and analytics applications, together with the alerting services that deliver warnings to health workers — consume these components rather than being defined by DPI-H.

This appendix provides a fuller breakdown of the individual capabilities within each of the five governance capability categories introduced in 3.4.5. It is illustrative reference material rather than a specification: the categories (clusters) are the level at which the reference architecture operates, and the detailed specification of any individual capability is a matter for dedicated standards efforts and national programmes. Across all five categories, three elements recur and belong to none of them exclusively — the roles that carry out governance (stakeholders, owners, and authors, both technical and clinical), the rules that determine when and how changes may be made, and the policy that frames them.

Stakeholder identification and analysis in Intake. Within the Intake category, stakeholder identification must vary according to the artefact type (code system, national extension, language translation, value set, concept map, logical information model, profile, or implementation guide) and the affected clinical, public-health, or administrative domain. Intake triage should require a structured stakeholder analysis covering authoritative agencies, clinicians across affected specialties and cadres, health programmes, implementers, analysts and statistical reporting leads, patients or affected communities, regulators, terminology specialists (including classification and clinical coding specialists), and data-protection or safety experts, ensuring that all parties impacted by a proposed change are engaged before authoring and review pathways are assigned.

Authoring and governance roles and separation of duties. Within Authoring and publication, collaborative authoring requires distinguishing six core operational roles alongside institutional governance roles, with explicit separation of duties according to artefact type:

  • Content author: drafts or updates candidate terminology concepts, value sets, mappings, data-model elements, or narrative guidance.
  • Domain authority (clinical specialty society, public-health programme authority, national classification centre, or regulatory agency): defines authoritative domain semantics, clinical appropriateness, classification conventions, and business rules for the affected domain, working alongside the programme owner who is accountable for programme indicators and service-delivery alignment.
  • Technical modeller (model authority / technical steward): designs and maintains logical information models, structural profiles, terminology bindings, and computable constraints in the LIMR.
  • Terminology specialist (terminology authority, including classification and clinical coding specialists): curates code systems, national extensions, translations, value sets, and concept maps in the Terminology Service, ensuring ontological, lexical, and statistical-classification integrity.
  • Reviewer: conducts independent domain/clinical, technical/implementability, and privacy/legal/ethical/equity evaluation of proposed artefacts against defined governance criteria.
  • Publisher (publication authority): verifies that all required review, consultation, and approval gates are complete, assigns version and provenance metadata, packages distributable releases, and publishes artefacts to operational endpoints under the oversight of the standards authority / governance body and for downstream implementers.

Separation of duties requires that the content author, technical modeller, or terminology specialist who drafts an artefact cannot act as its sole independent reviewer, domain approver, or publisher; for each artefact type, authoring is separated from independent review, domain/regulatory approval is separated from semantic/technical conformance sign-off, and final publication authority is exercised only after all required approvals are recorded.

RACI-style responsibility model across SGI capabilities. To make decision rights explicit across the five capability categories, the following RACI-style model (R = Responsible for execution; A = Accountable decision-maker with approval authority; C = Consulted prior to decision; I = Informed of outcome) assigns institutional and operational authorities to SGI capabilities:

prose:f-be46bc:
Within Authoring and publication, effective semantic governance requires that review, consultation, and approval capabilities be differentiated by expertise, impact, and institutional mandate rather than treated as a single generic sign-off:

  • Clinical and domain review. Clinical review cannot be treated as one uniform step because required expertise differs by medical or health specialty, profession, target population, care setting, and use case. Governance rules should define domain-specific reviewer qualifications (spanning relevant medical specialties, nursing, midwifery, pharmacy, laboratory medicine, public health, community health, and classification and clinical coding specialists), mandatory conflict-of-interest disclosure and recusal rules, multidisciplinary review panels where artefacts span multiple professions or programmes, and explicit quorum and decision rules before clinical sign-off is granted.
  • Technical and implementability review. Technical review must extend beyond syntactic or schema correctness to evaluate end-to-end implementability and validation, covering formal structural and profile validation, cross-artefact dependency and version-pinning checks, terminology binding and value-set expansion resolution, runtime performance and scalability impact, security and access-control considerations, backwards compatibility and data-migration pathways, validated implementation examples, and conformance-test readiness (including executable test fixtures and assertions).
  • Policy, legal, privacy, human-rights, ethical, and equity review. Because semantic artefacts may encode sensitive clinical classifications, stigmatising diagnoses, protected demographic or social attributes, benefit-eligibility or reimbursement restrictions, or mandatory surveillance concepts, artefacts with material individual or population impact require dedicated privacy, human-rights, legal, ethical, and health-equity review prior to approval to prevent discriminatory exclusion, unlawful data processing, or disproportionate surveillance harm.
  • Proportionate public consultation. Rather than leaving external consultation absent or purely optional, SGI governance should require proportionate public consultation for high-impact national artefacts (such as core national data models, mandated code systems and extensions, cross-programme value sets, and national implementation guides), providing accessible consultation materials (including plain-language summaries alongside technical artefacts), defined review windows, publication of submitted responses, and a transparent explanation of disposition for how comments were accepted, modified, or declined.
  • Approval authority and legal mandate. Approval authority must be explicitly tied to artefact ownership and legal or institutional mandate, defining who approves each artefact type (national extensions, translations, value sets, concept maps, logical models, and implementation guides) and separating clinical/programme approval, semantic and classification approval, technical and model approval, regulatory or statutory approval (where regulation, reimbursement, or mandatory reporting applies), and final publication approval where necessary, supported by documented conflict-resolution, escalation, appeals, and emergency change procedures.

The figure below illustrates how these capabilities relate in practice: a change moves from intake, through change management and publication, to monitoring, carried out by defined roles (stakeholders, authors, reviewers, domain and regulatory authorities, and publishers) and supported by tools (change-request tooling, authoring and repository services), with upstream content and management rules feeding the process.

Figure A.1 — Semantic governance capabilities, the roles that carry them out, and the supporting application components.

Automated structural validation versus expert review in Monitoring. In the Monitoring category (and throughout release validation), governance rules must explicitly distinguish automated structural validation from expert semantic, clinical, policy, safety, and implementation review. Automated validation — such as schema and profile conformance checks, canonical URI and dependency integrity, value-set expansion verification, concept-map structural checks, and automated staleness or drift detection — is essential for verifying formal syntactic and structural constraints consistently at scale, but it cannot establish clinical appropriateness, semantic equivalence of translations or mappings, legal or ethical acceptability, patient safety, or real-world usability. Continuous SGI monitoring must therefore combine automated structural checks with periodic and event-triggered expert semantic, clinical, classification/coding, policy, legal, patient-safety, and implementation review, using field uptake telemetry and implementer feedback to detect semantic drift, unsafe coding patterns, or usability barriers in deployed systems.

Table 53.

Term Description
Application Component A deployable, modular piece of software that provides a defined set of functionality and holds the data it manages, exposing both through services.
Application Service An explicitly defined unit of application behaviour. Anch application service exposes the functionality of an application component to its environment.
ArchiMate An open enterprise architecture modelling language, published by The Open Group, for describing and visualising an architecture across business, application and technology layers. The models in this guidance are written in ArchiMate.
Capability A high-level ability the health system possesses or needs in order to achieve its goals. It expresses what the health system is able to do, independently of how that ability is implemented.
Business Domain A specific focus area or subsystem within a broader business system, characterized by its own essential attributes [Under review]
Outcome An end result or consequence of a set of activities; an outcome is often measurable and signals progress towards a goal.
Product A concrete offering, bundling services and data, that is made available to stakeholders.
Business Services Layer (Business Services layer) A layer of the reference architecture grouping the health capabilities that national health systems strive to deliver across their principal domains — clinical care, public health, the health supply chain, and health financing — together with the shared components that enable them.
Client Members of the public who are potential or current users of health services, including health prevention and wellness activities.
Data Governance The structures and standards (policies & legal frameworks) necessary to coordinate and manage the data journey from collection, storage, sharing, analysis to use to produce trusted, secure and quality data for decision making
Data Object A defined unit of structured data used or produced by an application component.
Digital Health (digital health) The systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science, and data to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce, and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health and wellness.
Digital Infrastructure Infrastructures in the digital domain are digital resources, such as systems and specifications, built as shared means to achieve many ends
Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) A set of shared digital systems that should be secure and interoperable, and can be built on open standards and specifications to deliver and provide equitable access to public and/or private services at societal scale and are governed by applicable legal frameworks and enabling rules to drive development, inclusion, innovation, trust, and competition, while respecting human rights and fundamental freedoms. (G20/UNDP)
Enterprise Architecture (EA, enterprise architecture) The organising logic for business processes and IT infrastructure reflecting the integration and
standardisation requirements of the organisation's operating model. [Under review]
Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR, HL7 FHIR, HL7 FHIR®, FHIR®) FHIR is a standard for healthcare data exchange, published by HL7®
Foundational Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-F) Foundational Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-F) is the digital public infrastructure, such as identity, payments and data exchange, upon which the health sector can build. DPI-H is distinct from DPI-F and builds on it.
Functional Application (Functional application) Functional applications are application components that deliver a specific operational function within a defined domain. They are context-specific, reflecting the operational requirements of a programme, scheme, or institution that procures them.
Goal A high-level statement of intent, direction, or desired state for an organisation and its stakeholders.
Health Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-H, HDPI) Health Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-H) refers to digital resources that are built as a shared means for fulfilling multiple health agency functions.
Health Information Exchange (HIE) [To be included before publication]
Health Programme Health programmes are structured and coordinated interventions and services, delivered to defined populations or patient groups, to prevent disease, promote health, and address specific health needs.
Integration Bespoke capability of connecting one application component to another [Under review]
Interoperability (interoperability) Interoperability is the standards-based capability of heterogeneous information systems to communicate, exchange data, and use the exchanged information to execute functions effectively.
Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes (LOINC) LOINC is a common language (a set of identifiers, names, and codes) for identifying health measurements, observations, and documents.
Point-of-Service Applications (POS, Point-of-service applications, Point of Service Application, PoS) Point-of-service applications are end-user application components (IT systems or software tools) used by individuals directly engaged in healthcare—such as clinicians, community health workers, and patients—that enable interaction with the broader healthcare ecosystem. [Under review]
Reference Architecture (RA, reference architecture) A technology-neutral blueprint that captures the common building blocks, relationships, and design principles of a technical environment.
Registry (registry) A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, health products and/or the health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set. [Under review]
Repository
SMART Guidelines (SMART guidelines, SMART, Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines) Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines are a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital.
SNOMED CT (SNOMED, CT, SNOMED-CT, Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine - Clinical Terms, Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Clinical Terms) Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms is a structured clinical terminology standard for use in electronic health records.
SNOMED GPS (SNOMED-GPS, Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Global Patient Set, Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine-Global Patient Set, GPS) Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Global Patient Set is a list of basic clinical terms. It is an open and freely accessible subset of SNOMED CT terms that represents the breadth of concepts included in the SNOMED CT International Edition.
Solution Architecture The design of a specific application component or HDPI expressed through specifications and diagrams [Under review]
Stakeholder (stakeholder) An individual, role, or organisation with an interest in the outcomes of the architecture.
TOGAF The Open Group Architecture Framework, an enterprise architecture framework and method, published by The Open Group, for developing an enterprise architecture.
Value The benefit or utility a stakeholder gains from using a service, product, or capability.
Actor (Conformance Model) (Actor, actor (conformance model)) An Actor is an abstract, well-bounded role in the health information ecosystem that is defined entirely by the information-processing responsibilities it assumes and the interactions it participates in. An Actor is neither a software product nor an organisational unit.
Adverse Events Following Immunization (AEFI, Adverse effects following immunisation) Adverse effects following immunisation
Business Process (business process) A set of activities and tasks performed in coordination to achieve a specified business objective, or to deliver value in a specific way to a health service user. In the context of digitizing care pathways, this could include “health service user registration” and “referrals”, for example (see section 3.3).
Data Dictionary (data dictionary) A singular storage location for information about the data elements, detailing their type and definition, relationships, origin and use.
Data Element (data element) A unit of data that has a specific and precise meaning.
Deploy (deployment, Deployment) Make the software available for use beyond testing purposes.
Digital Transformation (digital transformation) The process of digitally optimizing and driving systems-level changes by leveraging innovation, analytics and feedback mechanisms to improve person-centred health systems. Digital technologies are used to fundamentally change and improve how health services are delivered and accessed across all health programme areas (12,14,15).
Digitalization (digitalization) The process of digitally automating and simplifying processes to streamline individual health programmes and reduce manual efforts for greater efficiency (12,13).
Digitization (digitization) The process of converting and organizing data from paper records into a digital format for easier entry, storage and retrieval (12,16).
End-User (End user, end user, end users) People who will be using the digital system(s).
Features (features) The characteristics of a system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g. “reporting” can be a feature of a PCPOSS).
Full-STAC (full-STAC, Full Standards, Technologies, Architectures, and Content) An ecosystem specifying open standards, open technologies, open architectures, and open content (full-STAC).
Functional Requirements (functional requirements, Functional requirements) Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified health system challenges (e.g. a PCPOSS must be able to remind health workers which health service users to follow-up with).
Functions (functions) Functions in a system are how features are implemented (e.g. “calculating aggregate data” and “displaying feedback in the form of diagrams” are functions of the “reporting” feature of a PCPOSS).
Generic Product (Generic product or product information, product information, generic national product code) In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information.
Governance (governance, governance (health supply chain)) Governance is the set of arrangements through which decision authority is distributed, exercised and accounted for across all those who depend upon, contribute to, or are served by the shared infrastructure.
International Telecommunication Union (ITU, International Telecommunications Union) International Telecommunication Union
Non-Functional Requirements (Non-functional requirements, nonfunctional requirements, NFR) General attributes and features of the digital system to ensure usability and overcome technical and physical constraints. Examples of non-functional requirements include ability to work offline, multiple language settings, and password protection (see section 3.8).
Open Architectures (open architectures) Open architectures refer to high-level specifications of technical designs that provide blueprints for creating open ecosystems structured into reusable and shareable components.
Open Content (open content) Open content refers to domain ideas and synthesized knowledge clearly documented without restrictions inhibiting readability or usage.
Open Source (Open-source software, open-source software, open source) Open-source software is software with source code that is published and made freely available to the public, enabling anyone to inspect, modify and enhance the code (18). While the source code is open to everyone, this does not mean that implementation of software is necessarily without costs. An open-source software must have a license approved by the Open Source Initiative (19).
Open Standards (open standards, Open standards) Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public, which are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (20).
Open Technologies (open technologies) Open technologies denote components of configurable and extensible source code — often curated as digital public goods — that perform distinct functions while adhering to open standards.
Organogram (organogram) A visual representation of an organization’s structure that shows the hierarchy of various roles and reporting relationships.
Product Master Data (PMD, product master data) Product master data consists of standardized information that accurately describes a health product’s characteristics. This data remains consistent across all instances of a product.
Request for Quotation (RFQ) Request for quotation
Supply Chain Information System Maturity Model (SCISMM, Supply Chain Information System Maturity Model (USAID), Supply Chain Information Systems Maturity Model) Supply Chain Information System Maturity Model (USAID)
Sustainable Development Goal (SDG, Sustainable Development Goals) Sustainable Development Goal
Systems Architecture (systems architecture, system architecture) The technical framework of the system depicted in a conceptual model that defines how the system is structured and how its elements are connected.
Total Cost of Ownership (TCO, total cost of ownership) The resources required to support a digital health intervention throughout its life cycle.
Traceability (traceability) The ability to trace something. In some cases, it is interpreted as the ability to verify the history, location or application of an item by means of documented identification (14).
Trade Item (trade item, Trade item) Trade items are manufacturer-specific branded health products that are identifiable and unique to a particular brand or manufacturer.
Use Case (use case) A use case is an example scenario of how the end-user will use the system.
User Acceptance Testing (UAT, User acceptance testing, User acceptance testing (UAT)) User acceptance testing (UAT) is conducted to see whether the end-users are satisfied with the end product (24).
User Persona (Persona, persona, user persona) A generic or archetypical profile of an end-user that is representative of a single type of end-user.
User Story (Requirements) (User Story, user story) Captures a long list of features from an end-user’s perspective. It describes who the end-user is, with their feature wants or needs, and the reason for that want or need (see section 3.2.3).
Workflow (workflow) The sequence of activities from one task to another (see section 3.3).
Enabling Environment (enabling environment) Attitudes, actions, policies and practices that stimulate and support effective and efficient functioning of organizations, individuals and programmes. The enabling environment includes legal, regulatory and policy frameworks and political, sociocultural, institutional and economic factors (3).
Evaluation (evaluation) The systematic and objective assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention with the aim of determining the fulfilment of objectives, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability (8).
Health Information System (HIS, health information system, Health Information System (HIS), Health Information Systems) A system that integrates data collection, processing, reporting, and use of the information necessary for improving health service effectiveness and efficiency through better management at all levels of health services.
Monitoring (monitoring) The continuous process of collecting and analysing data to compare how well an intervention is being implemented against expected results (8).
Client Registry (CR) The Client Registry is the national authoritative source of health-specific person identity. It is the foundational health-sector component that maintains a unique, verifiable identity record for every person who accesses or is eligible to access health services within a jurisdiction.
Health Facility Registry (FR, Facility Registry, HFR) The Health Facility Registry is the national authoritative source of identity, location, and classification data for all facilities, locations, and organisations through which health services are delivered or that are otherwise relevant to health system operations.
Health Workforce Registry (HWR, Health Worker Registry) The Health Workforce Registry is the national authoritative record of identity, credential, and classification data for all health workers recognised as part of the national health workforce — including licensed or certified clinical professionals, community health workers, allied health personnel, and administrative and management staff in health-related roles.
Product Registry (PR) The Product Registry is the national authoritative source of core identity and classification data for health products — medicines, vaccines, medical devices, diagnostics, and health commodities — recognised for use within a jurisdiction.
Terminology Service (TS) The Terminology Service is a governed, publicly accessible service that manages, publishes, and provides access to the standardised terminologies, code systems, value sets, and concept maps used across the digital health ecosystem.
Logical Information Model Repository (LIMR) The Logical Information Model Repository is a governed, publicly accessible repository and management platform for computable clinical and administrative information models that define the logical structure, semantics, and terminology bindings of health data objects across a national digital health ecosystem.
Lifelong Health Record (LHR) The Lifelong Health Record (LHR) is one or more governed data repositories, whether physically consolidated or virtually federated, that collectively maintain a longitudinal, person-centred record of an individual's key health information across care settings and over their lifetime.
Semantic Governance Infrastructure (SGI) The Semantic Governance Infrastructure (SGI) is the cross-cutting capability that keeps the metadata registry components accurate, consistent and trustworthy, so that the semantic consistency they are intended to provide does not degrade as the health digital ecosystem grows.
Computable Decision Support Engine (CDSE) The Computable Decision Support Engine is a governed, shared application component that delivers context-appropriate, evidence-based guidance at the point of clinical decision-making by applying computable clinical rules and knowledge artefacts to person-specific health data.
Supplier Registry (SR) The Supplier Registry is the authoritative master data source for identity, classification, and regulatory status of suppliers engaged in the health supply chain — including manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers, third-party logistics providers, importers, and procurement agents.
Benefits Package Registry (BPR) The Benefits Package Registry is the national authoritative record of all health benefit packages offered within a country's health financing ecosystem. It holds the definitive description of what each package covers, who is eligible in general terms, which scheme or schemes offer it, and under what rules and conditions benefits may be accessed.
Contract and Benefits Management System (CBMS, Contract & Benefits Management System)
Health Management Information System (HMIS) The Health Management Information System is a governed, shared application component responsible for the systematic collection, aggregation, analysis, and dissemination of population-level and facility-level health data to support health system planning, performance monitoring, resource allocation, and policy decision-making.
Public Health Surveillance Platform (PHSP) The Public Health Surveillance Platform is a governed, shared application component for the systematic, ongoing collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of health data to detect, monitor, and respond to public health threats and events.
